newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends week on positive note after payrolls, Rubin.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends week on positive note after payrolls, Rubin.

text.p: The dollar ended sharply higher against the yen and the mark on Friday, cheered by reassuring comments from U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and a U.S. employment report that suggested the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates again soon.

Rubin, in Japan on his way to a meeting of Asia-Pacific finance ministers in the Philippines, rejected suggestions that a stronger Japanese currency -- and thus a weaker U.S. dollar -- was the best way to avoid a renewed rise in Japan's trade surplus with the United States.
"We don't believe in anybody using their currency for trade policies -- us or anybody else," Rubin told reporters.
His remarks reassured investors who had feared that harsher rhetoric over Japan's burgeoning bilateral trade surplus would pressure the dollar.
The dollar ended the day at 124.30 yen, substantially up from 122.59 on Thursday. Against the mark, the dollar climbed to 1.6858 against Thursday's closing rate of 1.6695.

The dollar's strength was reinforced on Friday when the U.S. Labour Department released much-anticipated March employment data that showed a modest 175,000 jobs were added to the U.S. economy in March -- below Wall Street consensus forecasts.

But the data also showed a further decline in the unemployment rate to 5.2 percent and sizable wage gains -- both signals that Fed policy-makers could follow up last week's interest rate hike with another in May to head off inflation.

"I don't think it was the payrolls number so much as it was the wages," said John Hazelton, chief dealer at Manufacturers and Traders Bank. "That's something that the Fed said they would monitor closely and when that showed an increase, expectations of higher rates drove the dollar up."

Average hourly earnings rose by five cents for the second consecutive month in March -- from $12.10 to $12.15. Over the past year, the report showed that hourly wages have risen 4 percent, the biggest rise since the 12 months ended June 1990.

Once again, the dollar performed admirably in the face of U.S. market volatility on Friday. The Dow industrials slumped in the aftermath of the payrolls report and traded lower for much of the session before popping higher in the late afternoon to end up 49 points at 6,526.
The yield of the bellwether 30-year Treasury bond, which moves in the opposite direction of its price, rose to a seven-month high of 7.14 percent before recouping some losses in late trading.

"We're not really following the asset markets and instead seeing more interest to buy the dollar on the interest rate outlook," said Lizbeth Goldberg, assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Bayerische Hypotheken und Wechselbank.

The dollar was also helped late in the day by comments from Federal Reserve Vice Chair Alice Rivlin, who said in a speech on Friday that the strong dollar was clearly helping keep U.S. inflation subdued.
Dealers said the remarks encouraged buying of dollars by demonstrating that U.S. officials are content with the dollar at its current strong levels.
In other trading on Friday, the dollar pushed up to a fresh two-year high against the Canadian dollar before ending at C$1.3921, just below Thursday's close of C$1.3926.
The dollar settled at 1.4425 Swiss francs against 1.4345 on Thursday, while the British pound shrank to $1.6345 after closing on Thursday at $1.6452.
